To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) there has been an increase in the inequality of joblessness in the United Kingdom, (ii) this is largely within group, not between group, (iii) it is not due to the increasing size of the household or to the changing characteristics of the household, and (iv) it is not related to any other observable characteristic of the household.

(a) the polarization of the British labour market has increased substantially over the last 20 years, and (b) this polarization is not primarily due to changes in the size of household or to the characteristics of individuals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the distributional consequences of labour market performance.
the measurement of polarization in the distribution of labour market outcomes and the identification of its sources.
the measurement of inequality in the distribution and incidence of work.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is not strong enough to support the claim that the distribution of work has become more unequal over the period of our study.
there is no evidence that the polarization of work has increased in the United Kingdom.
the UK has made progress in reducing unemployment and in increasing employment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the distribution of work in Britain has become increasingly polarized over the past decade and a half, with the largest changes being within groups and unrelated to the size of the household.
the polarization index is a good measure of polarization.

the polarization of the distribution of work in Britain is not a recent phenomenon and is not primarily a consequence of the changing composition of the population or of the changing structure of the household economy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
inequality and polarization in the distribution of employment can be measured and quantified in a way that is both theoretically consistent and practically applicable.
the distribution of work has become more unequal over the last two decades.

there is no single measure of joblessness that captures all aspects of labour market performance, and that it is important to consider the extent and sources of inequality in the distribution in order to understand the implications of aggregate joblessness for different groups of workers.
